screens.title: Controller-Based Input vs Direct Hand Tracking
screens.narratorSegment: Controllers and hand tracking both let users manipulate virtual objects, but they differ in reliability, feedback, and use cases. Controller-based input uses physical handheld devices that provide buttons, triggers, joysticks, and haptic feedback. These devices are tracked in 3D space and provide precise discrete input such as a trigger press. That precision makes controllers ideal for fast-paced or highly precise manipulation where button state is fundamental. By contrast, direct hand tracking uses cameras on the headset to detect real hand poses and joint positions, giving a more natural, controller-free experience. Hand tracking excels at intuitive gestures like grabbing or pinching without an intermediary device, but it can be less precise in fast motions or occluded views. A common misconception is thinking hand tracking always replaces controllers; in practice they complement each other. Designers often offer both: controllers for precision tasks and hands for exploration, or fall back to controllers when tracking is unreliable. As you design interactions, think about feedback: controllers offer haptic confirmation, while hand-tracked interactions need clear visual feedback such as pose changes or object highlighting so users understand when a grab registers. Which approach you choose shapes how you map actions and where you add safeguards for safety and precision.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Input Comparison
Controller-Based Input
  • Provides buttons, triggers, sticks and haptics for discrete and precise input.
  • Tracked in 3D for pointing and accurate position-based grabs.
  • Ideal for fast-paced or physics-dependent interactions.
Common misconception
Controllers feel less natural, but they often provide the precision and feedback needed for reliable gameplay.
Direct Hand Tracking
  • Uses headset cameras to detect hand joints and finger poses.
  • Enables natural gestures like pinches and open-hand grabs without controllers.
  • Less precise in occlusion or fast motion; needs strong visual feedback.
Design tip
Add highlights and pose changes to indicate when a grab or pinch is recognized since there is no haptic feedback.
Practical example

Offer both methods: allow controller grip to pick up a tool, but support a pinch gesture for toggling UI or inspection. Fall back to controllers when hand joints are not reliably tracked.

screens.title: Configuring the Input Action System
screens.narratorSegment: Unity's Input Action System moves you from polling hardware to listening for abstract actions that represent intent. Start by creating an Input Action Asset in the Project window and open it. Define Action Maps such as LeftHand and RightHand to group related actions. Inside a map add actions like Grab, Select, or Move. For each action add bindings that map to specific physical controls, for example binding Grab to the grip button on a left controller using a path like a left XRController grip binding. Save the asset and assign it to the Input Action Manager on your XR Origin so the XR Controller components can reference actions by name. The advantage is you now listen for an action rather than a specific device state. A common mistake is leaving actions unassigned in the XR Controller component—this results in no response despite correct bindings in the asset. Another issue is forgetting distinct action maps for left and right hands, which complicates handedness logic. As you build your asset, test each binding in Play mode: confirm pressing the physical control triggers the mapped action and that the XR Controller shows the correct Select or Grab action is linked.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Input Action Setup
Steps to create bindings
  1. Create an Input Action Asset in Project window (Create > Input Actions).
  2. Add Action Maps like LeftHand and RightHand.
  3. Add Actions such as Grab and Select inside each map.
  4. Add Bindings that point to the physical input paths for your controllers.
  5. Assign the asset to the Input Action Manager on XR Origin and link actions in XR Controller components.
Common mistake
Leaving the XR Controller's Select or Grab Action unassigned even after setting up the asset; always verify the link in the Inspector.
Example binding
// In the Input Action Asset UI
Action Map: XRI LeftHand
  Action: Grab
    Binding: <XRController>{LeftHand}/gripButton

// Assign this asset to Input Action Manager, then set XR Controller -> Grab Action to this action.
Key Takeaway

Treat actions as intent. Bindings connect that intent to hardware so your interaction code stays device-agnostic.

screens.title: XR Grab Interactable Essentials
screens.narratorSegment: The XR Grab Interactable is the XR Interaction Toolkit component that makes a GameObject respond to grab interactions. For it to work correctly you must add a Collider and a Rigidbody. The Collider lets the XR Grab Interactor detect proximity and contact; the Rigidbody lets physics govern motion when the object is released or thrown. When grabbed, the Interactable may become kinematic or follow the interactor depending on attachment settings. Kinematic attachment is useful for objects that should move exactly with the controller for a stable weld. Velocity Tracking attachment records motion so when you release the Rigidbody continues with realistic throw velocity. A common error is forgetting the Rigidbody, which prevents proper physics handoff and throws. Another pitfall is using incorrect layer masks or interaction layer masks that stop the XR Grab Interactor from seeing the object. You can also customize attachment points by adding a child transform to act as the pivot for where the object grips. Understanding these pieces ensures grabs feel responsive, predictable, and physically correct in Play mode. XR Grab Interactable Essentials means collider + rigidbody + xr grab interactable are required; pick attachment mode to choose between fixed-weld or physics-driven throws.. In practical terms, what the component requires and how attachment types change behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › XR Grab Interactable
Required components
  • Collider — enables proximity and contact detection.
  • Rigidbody — enables physics simulation on release and throwing.
  • XR Grab Interactable — handles attach/detach and event hooks.
Attachment modes
Kinematic: object follows exactly. Velocity Tracking: records motion for realistic throws.
Example: Preparing an Interactable Cube
1. Create Cube
2. Add Box Collider (auto)
3. Add Rigidbody
4. Add XR Grab Interactable
5. Test: grab, move, release, throw

Troubleshoot: if cube doesn't respond, check Interaction Layer Masks and missing Rigidbody.
Common mistake
Not adding a Rigidbody prevents the object from being thrown with realistic physics — add one and verify mass and drag.

screens.title: Wiring Grab Action to XR Controller Components
screens.narratorSegment: Once you have an Input Action Asset and an XR Origin with XR Controller components, the next step is linking a Grab action to the controller so the toolkit knows when to begin a grab. In the Inspector of your LeftHand Controller component find the Grab Action or Select Action field and choose the corresponding action from your Input Action Asset—usually under XRI LeftHand/Grab. Repeat for the right hand using the RightHand map. This makes the XR Grab Interactor respond when the physical button is pressed. A practical example is to create a Grab action bound to the grip button and a Select action bound to the trigger. Then assign the asset to the Input Action Manager on XR Origin so both controllers reference the same asset. If you prefer code, you can also read the action performed event and call interaction methods, but using the XR Controller fields reduces boilerplate. Always test in Play mode: press the controller button and ensure the interactor enters select state and picks up the grabbable object. If nothing happens, check that the Input Action Asset is assigned to Input Action Manager and that the action path matches the controller hardware.

  2. In LeftHand Controller component set Grab Action to XRI LeftHand/Grab.

// Pseudocode outline to visualize wiring
// 1) Create Input Action Asset with Grab
// 2) Assign asset to Input Action Manager

screens.title: Testing Grab & Release Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Testing grab and release behavior ensures objects move naturally when the user interacts. Start Play mode with controllers connected, approach the grabbable object and press the configured Grab button. Observe whether the object follows the controller immediately or records motion for a throw. If it is set to kinematic attachment it will stay rigidly attached to the controller transform, which is useful for tools that must align exactly. If set to velocity tracking, test releasing while moving your hand to confirm the Rigidbody picks up velocity and the object throws. Check the Rigidbody settings — mass, drag, and interpolation — because unrealistic mass or high drag can make throws feel weak. Also verify the Collider fits the object shape; a very large collider can cause early grabs or collisions. A frequent trap is incorrect Interaction Layer Mask on either interactor or interactable, so the interactor cannot detect the object. Fix this by ensuring the object's layer is included in the interactor's mask. After testing both pick-up and throw, try grabbing with different velocities to confirm behavior is predictable and stable.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Testing Grabs
Checklist for playtesting
  • Verify object has Collider and Rigidbody.
  • Confirm XR Grab Interactable is present and configured for attachment type.
  • Test grabbing, moving, and releasing at different speeds.
  • Tune Rigidbody mass and drag for believable throws.
Troubleshoot
If the object doesn't respond, check the Interaction Layer Mask on the interactor and the object's layer.
Scenario card
Throw test

Grab the cube, accelerate your hand, then release. Observe flight and collisions. If it drops too quickly, reduce drag; if it clips, adjust collider or interpolation settings.

Key Takeaway

Realistic behavior requires both correct attachment mode and tuned Rigidbody parameters.

screens.title: Enable Hand Tracking for Meta Quest
screens.narratorSegment: To prepare your Unity project for Meta Quest hand tracking you need to enable the platform plugin and set the proper options in Project Settings. Open Edit then Project Settings and choose XR Plug-in Management. Under the Android tab enable the Oculus provider. Next find the Meta XR SDK or Oculus XR Plugin settings in Project Settings. Set Tracking Origin Mode to Floor to align the tracked hands with the room scale floor origin. In Features enable Hand Tracking Support and set it to Supported or Required depending on your needs. Marking it as Supported allows fallback to controllers. Enabling the backend does not automatically visualize hands; you must integrate SDK hand prefabs to see the user’s hands. Also note safety and design considerations: hand tracking removes physical controllers, so warn players to clear their play space and design interactions that minimize accidental strikes. After enabling the plugin and features, run a build on the device or test with a connected headset and verify that joint data is available to the runtime. If joint data is missing, double-check the plugin enablement and that hand tracking is allowed in headset settings.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Enable Hand Tracking
Step-by-step
  1. Open Project Settings → XR Plug-in Management → Android and enable Oculus.
  2. Open Meta XR SDK (or Oculus XR Plugin) settings in Project Settings.
  3. Set Tracking Origin Mode to Floor.
  4. Under Features set Hand Tracking Support to Supported or Required.
  5. Build to device or test with headset to confirm joint data.
Notes & safety

Hand tracking removes physical controllers. Warn users to clear their play area and design clear visual feedback to show when interactions will occur.

Integration note
Enabling engine support is only the backend step; visualizing hands requires SDK hand prefabs or custom integration with the XR Interaction Toolkit.

screens.title: Visualizing Hands with SDK Prefabs
screens.narratorSegment: Visualizing tracked hands makes hand tracking usable because users see where their fingers are and whether gestures register. Meta provides SDK-specific hand prefabs that instantiate hand models and populate joint transforms. To visualize hands, import the Meta XR SDK hand prefabs into your project and add them under the XR Origin in place of controller models. These prefabs often include components that expose joint transforms and higher-level scripts for tracking. Importantly, visualization alone does not provide interaction: the hand prefab needs XR Interactor components on child objects that represent interaction points such as a palm or finger tip. For example, adding an XR Direct Interactor to a palm object enables direct grabbing when the palm contacts a grabbable object. For pinch-style interactions, add an interactor to a fingertip child. A common integration mistake is only adding visuals without attachable interactor components, so hands appear but cannot select or grab. When you add these interactors, configure Interaction Layer Masks and any Grab Actions that will be used for gesture-driven selection. Finally, test in Play mode to confirm that both the visual model and interactor points update with joint data and can manipulate XR Grab Interactable objects.

screens.title: Gesture Recognition Basics
screens.narratorSegment: Gesture recognition translates joint data into meaningful user intents like a pinch or a grab. The simplest approach is rule-based: monitor positions of relevant joints such as the index tip and thumb tip. To detect a pinch, measure the distance between those two tips and trigger when the value falls below a threshold. For a closed-hand grab, check that all finger joint curls exceed a threshold or that the distance between fingertips and palm is below a limit. Use the hand tracking SDK's provided joint transforms, for example thumbTip and indexTip, and compute distance in world or local hand space. Implement smoothing and hysteresis to avoid noisy toggles: require the threshold to be crossed for a small time or use a slightly lower release threshold to prevent flicker. Remember hand tracking data can be less precise than controller states; expect occasional false positives and add visual confirmation like a highlighted object or a hand pose change. A common mistake is using raw instantaneous values without smoothing, which leads to jittery recognition. With a small rule-based system you can add gesture-driven interactions while maintaining clear feedback for the user.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Gesture Recognition
Simple pinch detection
// Conceptual steps
1. Read thumbTip and indexTip joint positions
2. float d = Vector3.Distance(thumbTip, indexTip)
3. if (d < pinchThreshold) => pinch detected
4. Add smoothing and a release threshold to prevent flicker
Smoothing tip
Use a running average or require the threshold to hold for a few frames before firing the gesture event.
Example scenario

Detect a pinch to pick up a small UI object. Show a highlighted outline and a hand pose change when the pinch registers to give clear feedback.

Gotcha
Hand tracking is noisier than controllers. Without smoothing and feedback, gestures can feel unreliable.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Common Integration Issues
screens.narratorSegment: When things don't work as expected, the issues often fall into predictable categories. If virtual hands appear but cannot interact with XR Grab Interactable objects, the likely cause is that the hand prefab lacks XR Interactor components on the appropriate child transforms. Visuals alone provide no interaction. Add XR Direct Interactor or XR Ray Interactor components to fingertip or palm objects depending on the interaction style. Another frequent problem is missing Rigidbody on grabbable objects; without it throws and physics-based behaviors won't work. Interaction Layer Masks are another source of issues: if the interactor's mask doesn't include the object's layer, detection fails silently. Input Action misconfiguration can also block interaction: ensure the Input Action Asset is assigned to the Input Action Manager and that XR Controller components reference the correct actions. For hand gestures, noisy joint data can cause flicker; use smoothing and hysteresis to make gestures stable. Finally, platform settings matter: if the Oculus provider is not enabled under XR Plug-in Management, the runtime will not supply hand joint data. Systematic checking of these areas resolves most integration problems quickly.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we will connect practical Unity workflow with the user-facing experience of interacting in VR. You will learn to treat input as an abstraction: defining actions like “Grab” and binding them to controllers or hand gestures. We will add XR Grab Interactable components so objects can be picked up, thrown, and returned to physics when released. Then we enable headset hand tracking, and explore how to visualize hands using provided SDK prefabs. Finally, we examine basic gesture recognition — for example, detecting a pinch by checking the distance between index tip and thumb tip — and discuss common pitfalls such as missing Rigidbody components or absent interactor scripts on hand prefabs. This chapter matters because input design directly shapes whether an experience feels precise or frustrating. A robust Input Action configuration makes your project portable across controller types, while hand tracking can increase immersion but requires careful feedback and safety considerations. By the end you’ll be able to wire a grab action, test it with controllers, and prepare your project to display tracked hands and detect simple gestures.

Across this chapter you will practice four concrete skills that form the foundation for responsive VR interactions. First, you will understand the difference between controller-based input and direct hand tracking: controllers provide hardware buttons, triggers and haptics, while tracked hands give camera-based finger and joint data. Second, you will configure Unity's Input Action System to map physical controller inputs to reusable actions such as Grab and Select, making your code portable across controller types. Third, you will implement grab and release mechanics: adding XR Grab Interactable to objects along with Collider and Rigidbody so they can be held, thrown, and returned to physics. Finally, you will prepare and visualize hand tracking on supported headsets by enabling the platform plugin and optionally instantiating SDK hand prefabs. Each objective includes a small milestone you can verify: mapping a Grab action, picking up a cube, enabling hand tracking in Project Settings, and detecting a simple pinch. We will also discuss why each step matters and common mistakes to avoid, so you leave with practical, verifiable skills.

We will use four verifiable milestones to prove competency. For input abstraction, bind a 'Grab' action in an Input Action Asset and link it to your XR Controller component; this shows you can replace hardware without rewriting logic. For grab mechanics, make an Interactable Cube with XR Grab Interactable, a Collider and a Rigidbody, then pick it up in Play mode — this proves you understand physics-driven grabbing and attachment types like kinematic or velocity tracking. For hand tracking, enable the Oculus provider under XR Plug-in Management, set Tracking Origin Mode to Floor, and mark Hand Tracking Support as Supported or Required; this confirms the runtime will provide joint data. For gesture recognition, write a simple script that reads thumb and index tip positions and logs a pinch when they are close; that demonstrates using joint positions for interaction. Each milestone targets a practical gap: many developers forget the Rigidbody, or visualize hands without adding interactors. Completing these checks builds reliable, testable interaction features.

Controllers and hand tracking both let users manipulate virtual objects, but they differ in reliability, feedback, and use cases. Controller-based input uses physical handheld devices that provide buttons, triggers, joysticks, and haptic feedback. These devices are tracked in 3D space and provide precise discrete input such as a trigger press. That precision makes controllers ideal for fast-paced or highly precise manipulation where button state is fundamental. By contrast, direct hand tracking uses cameras on the headset to detect real hand poses and joint positions, giving a more natural, controller-free experience. Hand tracking excels at intuitive gestures like grabbing or pinching without an intermediary device, but it can be less precise in fast motions or occluded views. A common misconception is thinking hand tracking always replaces controllers; in practice they complement each other. Designers often offer both: controllers for precision tasks and hands for exploration, or fall back to controllers when tracking is unreliable. As you design interactions, think about feedback: controllers offer haptic confirmation, while hand-tracked interactions need clear visual feedback such as pose changes or object highlighting so users understand when a grab registers. Which approach you choose shapes how you map actions and where you add safeguards for safety and precision.

Unity's Input Action System moves you from polling hardware to listening for abstract actions that represent intent. Start by creating an Input Action Asset in the Project window and open it. Define Action Maps such as LeftHand and RightHand to group related actions. Inside a map add actions like Grab, Select, or Move. For each action add bindings that map to specific physical controls, for example binding Grab to the grip button on a left controller using a path like a left XRController grip binding. Save the asset and assign it to the Input Action Manager on your XR Origin so the XR Controller components can reference actions by name. The advantage is you now listen for an action rather than a specific device state. A common mistake is leaving actions unassigned in the XR Controller component—this results in no response despite correct bindings in the asset. Another issue is forgetting distinct action maps for left and right hands, which complicates handedness logic. As you build your asset, test each binding in Play mode: confirm pressing the physical control triggers the mapped action and that the XR Controller shows the correct Select or Grab action is linked.

The XR Grab Interactable is the XR Interaction Toolkit component that makes a GameObject respond to grab interactions. For it to work correctly you must add a Collider and a Rigidbody. The Collider lets the XR Grab Interactor detect proximity and contact; the Rigidbody lets physics govern motion when the object is released or thrown. When grabbed, the Interactable may become kinematic or follow the interactor depending on attachment settings. Kinematic attachment is useful for objects that should move exactly with the controller for a stable weld. Velocity Tracking attachment records motion so when you release the Rigidbody continues with realistic throw velocity. A common error is forgetting the Rigidbody, which prevents proper physics handoff and throws. Another pitfall is using incorrect layer masks or interaction layer masks that stop the XR Grab Interactor from seeing the object. You can also customize attachment points by adding a child transform to act as the pivot for where the object grips. Understanding these pieces ensures grabs feel responsive, predictable, and physically correct in Play mode. XR Grab Interactable Essentials means collider + rigidbody + xr grab interactable are required; pick attachment mode to choose between fixed-weld or physics-driven throws.. In practical terms, what the component requires and how attachment types change behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Once you have an Input Action Asset and an XR Origin with XR Controller components, the next step is linking a Grab action to the controller so the toolkit knows when to begin a grab. In the Inspector of your LeftHand Controller component find the Grab Action or Select Action field and choose the corresponding action from your Input Action Asset—usually under XRI LeftHand/Grab. Repeat for the right hand using the RightHand map. This makes the XR Grab Interactor respond when the physical button is pressed. A practical example is to create a Grab action bound to the grip button and a Select action bound to the trigger. Then assign the asset to the Input Action Manager on XR Origin so both controllers reference the same asset. If you prefer code, you can also read the action performed event and call interaction methods, but using the XR Controller fields reduces boilerplate. Always test in Play mode: press the controller button and ensure the interactor enters select state and picks up the grabbable object. If nothing happens, check that the Input Action Asset is assigned to Input Action Manager and that the action path matches the controller hardware.

Testing grab and release behavior ensures objects move naturally when the user interacts. Start Play mode with controllers connected, approach the grabbable object and press the configured Grab button. Observe whether the object follows the controller immediately or records motion for a throw. If it is set to kinematic attachment it will stay rigidly attached to the controller transform, which is useful for tools that must align exactly. If set to velocity tracking, test releasing while moving your hand to confirm the Rigidbody picks up velocity and the object throws. Check the Rigidbody settings — mass, drag, and interpolation — because unrealistic mass or high drag can make throws feel weak. Also verify the Collider fits the object shape; a very large collider can cause early grabs or collisions. A frequent trap is incorrect Interaction Layer Mask on either interactor or interactable, so the interactor cannot detect the object. Fix this by ensuring the object's layer is included in the interactor's mask. After testing both pick-up and throw, try grabbing with different velocities to confirm behavior is predictable and stable.

To prepare your Unity project for Meta Quest hand tracking you need to enable the platform plugin and set the proper options in Project Settings. Open Edit then Project Settings and choose XR Plug-in Management. Under the Android tab enable the Oculus provider. Next find the Meta XR SDK or Oculus XR Plugin settings in Project Settings. Set Tracking Origin Mode to Floor to align the tracked hands with the room scale floor origin. In Features enable Hand Tracking Support and set it to Supported or Required depending on your needs. Marking it as Supported allows fallback to controllers. Enabling the backend does not automatically visualize hands; you must integrate SDK hand prefabs to see the user’s hands. Also note safety and design considerations: hand tracking removes physical controllers, so warn players to clear their play space and design interactions that minimize accidental strikes. After enabling the plugin and features, run a build on the device or test with a connected headset and verify that joint data is available to the runtime. If joint data is missing, double-check the plugin enablement and that hand tracking is allowed in headset settings.

Visualizing tracked hands makes hand tracking usable because users see where their fingers are and whether gestures register. Meta provides SDK-specific hand prefabs that instantiate hand models and populate joint transforms.
